patient.name: Patricia Doyle
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then Intensive Care Unit
patient.complaint: Fever, rigors and yellow skin for 2 days; now drowsy and breathless
background: Metastatic pancreatic cancer; biliary stent placed 3 months ago
Lives with her daughter in Lewisham

diagnosis.exam: Expect a septic, trauma or pancreatitis patient who then develops failure of several organs (rising creatinine, hypoxaemia, confusion, hypotension), asking 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or what process explains the new findings.

points: Patricia, 72, has **metastatic pancreatic cancer** and a biliary stent.
Two days of fever, **rigors** and right upper quadrant pain.
Her daughter noticed **yellow eyes** and new confusion this morning.
She is breathless and has barely passed urine since yesterday.

visual.title: Where the infection started
visual.caption: RUQ pain, fever and jaundice with a blocked stent: **ascending cholangitis**. This is the source of her sepsis.

steps.lead: Patricia's infected stent caused sepsis. Once **two or more organ systems** fail, sepsis has become **MODS**.

steps.title: First bloods and gas
steps.text: Kidney, liver, lungs, circulation and clotting are all affected. **Lactate 6.2** shows poor tissue perfusion.

steps.lead: Patricia has the classic set: **shock**, renal failure, respiratory failure, hepatic injury, confusion, low urine output and a **raised lactate**.

steps.q: Patricia has sepsis plus hypotension, AKI, hypoxaemia, jaundice and confusion. Which term best describes her state?
steps.r: Failure of **two or more organ systems** from a systemic inflammatory response is MODS. The other labels each explain only part of the picture.

steps.title: Which of Patricia's organs are failing?
head: System
Sign of failure
Patricia

steps.title: From infection to MODS
nodes: Two or more organs fail = MODS
steps.caption: Sepsis is the commonest trigger; trauma and major illness (e.g. pancreatitis) do the same.

steps.lead: With five systems involved, Patricia's risk of death is very high. If her organs keep worsening despite treatment, MODS is progressing.

visual.title: Number of organ systems failing
visual.label: Patricia 5
visual.caption: One failed organ is not MODS. From **two** upwards, each extra organ adds a big step in mortality.

steps.text: If the stem lists several failing organs and asks for **one** diagnosis, do not pick 'acute kidney injury' or 'delirium'. Those are parts of the picture; **MODS** is the whole.
Sepsis plus organ failure = MODS. The three systems hit most often are **respiratory, renal and cardiovascular**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' where the answer is a **lactate** (perfusion) or blood cultures (cause), or a question on which organ-specific test shows which failure.

points: Resus team takes bloods, an arterial gas and blood cultures.
A urinary catheter drains only 10 mL in the first hour.
Portable chest X-ray is requested for her breathlessness.

steps.lead: No single test 'proves' MODS. Patricia's diagnosis is **clinical**, backed by evidence that each organ is failing.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas (on 15 L/min oxygen)
steps.text: **Lactic metabolic acidosis** from poor perfusion, plus hypoxaemia even on high-flow oxygen: respiratory failure.

visual.title: Patricia's lactate
visual.label: Patricia 6.2
visual.caption: Lactate is the **critical** blood test: it reflects tissue hypoperfusion. Repeat it to see if resuscitation is working.

steps.lead: Patricia gets the full set: **lactate**, FBC, U&Es, LFTs; creatinine, bilirubin and ABG for each organ; blood cultures and imaging to find the cause.

steps.q: Which investigation, taken before antibiotics, is most useful to identify the cause of Patricia's MODS?
steps.r: MODS is usually driven by sepsis, so **blood cultures** (and imaging of the source) find the cause. Biopsies have no place in the acute phase.

visual.title: Portable chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral diffuse shadowing with a normal heart size: lung injury from the systemic inflammation (ARDS pattern), not a single pneumonia.

steps.text: Lactate is used twice: once to show **how bad** perfusion is, then repeatedly to show **whether resuscitation is working**.
A normal-looking SpO2 on high-flow oxygen does not rule out respiratory failure. Use the **arterial blood gas** to measure hypoxia.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (treat the cause: IV antibiotics), which organ support fits which failure (dialysis, ventilation, vasopressors), and capacity or ceiling-of-care questions in terminal illness.

points: Sepsis Six started within the hour: oxygen, cultures, fluids, lactate, urine output.
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics given; gastroenterology plan to replace the blocked stent.
After 1.5 L of fluid her BP is still 82/50 mmHg.

steps.lead: The cause is sepsis, so Patricia's first-line treatment is **IV antibiotics** plus fixing the source (the blocked stent).

steps.q: Patricia stays hypotensive after adequate fluids. Which is the most appropriate next step?
steps.r: Cardiovascular failure despite fluids needs **vasopressors** (noradrenaline) in ICU. More fluid will flood her already injured lungs.

steps.lead: In ICU Patricia gets oxygen, fluids and **noradrenaline**, with continuous monitoring and **repeat lactates**. Each failing organ gets its own support.

steps.title: Organ support in MODS
head: Failing system
Support
rows: Treat the cause; continuous monitoring; repeat lactate

visual.title: Patricia's first 12 hours
visual.caption: Lactate improves on noradrenaline, but urine output stops: the kidneys keep failing. **Worsening organ function despite treatment** = progression.

points: Day 2: anuric, potassium 6.8, needs **dialysis**; intubated for hypoxia.
Sedated and ventilated, she can no longer make decisions.
No advance decision or lasting power of attorney exists.
Her oncologist confirms the cancer is terminal.

steps.lead: Patricia now **lacks capacity** and has a terminal illness. The team must discuss further escalation versus **palliative care** with her daughter.

steps.q: What is the most appropriate next step about further escalation for Patricia?
o: Ask her daughter to sign a consent form
Discuss escalation versus palliative care with her family and team
steps.r: Without capacity, decide in her **best interests** after discussion with family and the team. Family cannot sign consent for her (no LPA).

steps.lead: Because sepsis is the trigger, Patricia's care follows the **Surviving Sepsis Campaign** and **NICE sepsis** guidance.

steps.text: Giving more and more fluid to a patient with failing kidneys and lungs causes **fluid overload** and pulmonary oedema. Once fluids fail, move to **vasopressors**.
Match the support to the organ: kidneys = **dialysis**, lungs = **ventilation**, circulation = **vasopressors**. The cause is treated first (antibiotics for sepsis).

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why organs fail after sepsis, trauma or pancreatitis (systemic inflammation, microvascular dysfunction), why lactate rises, or why organs fail despite a normal BP.

steps.lead: Patricia's cholangitis triggered a severe systemic inflammatory response. Microvascular dysfunction starved her organs of blood, and they failed one after another.

points: Day 2: on noradrenaline her BP is **112/66 mmHg**.
Yet her lactate is still 3.9 and her kidneys have stopped.

steps.lead: Patricia's BP looks fine, but her **microcirculation** is still damaged, so organs keep failing despite a normal macrocirculation.

steps.q: Why is Patricia's lactate still raised despite a normal BP?
o: Her liver produces too much glucose
steps.r: Cytokine damage to the **endothelium** blocks flow in small vessels, independent of BP. Cells lack oxygen and make lactate.

steps.lead: Patricia's lactate tracks how much of her tissue is still short of oxygen. A falling trend means resuscitation is working.
Patricia's anuric kidneys caused fluid overload, which worsened her lungs. Each failing organ makes the next one worse.

steps.title: Why one failure leads to another
steps.caption: This interconnection is why mortality climbs so steeply with each extra organ.

steps.text: Exam phrase: organ failure after pancreatitis, trauma or sepsis is explained by a **systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) with multi-organ dysfunction**, not by one local complication.

o: Failure of two or more organ systems
Fever with a raised white cell count
Infection with a positive blood culture
mcq.r: MODS = failure of **two or more** organ systems, usually from a systemic inflammatory response.

mcq.q: What is the most common underlying cause of MODS?
mcq.r: **Sepsis** is the commonest trigger; trauma and major illness also cause it.

mcq.q: Which three systems are most commonly affected in MODS?
mcq.r: **Respiratory, renal and cardiovascular** failure are the most common.

mcq.q: What happens to mortality as more organs fail?
o: It rises sharply from two or more organs
It rises only after five organs
mcq.r: Mortality rises **sharply** once two or more organ systems have failed.

mcq.q: Which blood marker is critical for assessing perfusion in MODS?
mcq.r: **Lactate** reflects tissue hypoperfusion and is repeated to monitor response.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing MODS?
o: Clinical diagnosis with evidence of organ dysfunction
mcq.r: MODS is a **clinical diagnosis** backed by evidence of organ dysfunction.

mcq.q: What organ support is used for renal failure in MODS?
What is the first-line treatment of MODS caused by sepsis?
mcq.r: Treat the underlying cause: **antibiotics** for sepsis.

mcq.q: Why can organs fail in MODS even with a normal blood pressure?
mcq.r: Cytokine damage to the **endothelium** impairs microcirculatory flow independent of BP.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man is on the surgical ward 1 day after a laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid colon. He is confused and breathless and has passed 40 mL of urine in 4 hours. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 80/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. His creatinine has risen from 82 to 290 µmol/L and his bilirubin is 74 µmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: One diagnosis is wanted, so find the label that explains **every** abnormality, not just one.
Faecal peritonitis gives sepsis. Then circulation, kidneys, lungs, liver and brain all fail.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis plus failure of two or more organ systems: **multi-organ dysfunction syndrome**.

elim: AKI is present but explains only the kidneys, not the hypoxia, jaundice or shock.
Cardiogenic shock follows a heart problem; here there is fever and a septic source.
Hepatorenal syndrome occurs in advanced liver disease; he has none.
PE gives hypoxia and shock but not fever, jaundice and a septic source.

steps.x: **D. MODS.** Rule: several organs failing after sepsis, trauma or pancreatitis = MODS.

technique.stem: A 57 year old woman with pyelonephritis is drowsy and hypotensive despite a fluid bolus. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. Her creatinine is rising and her urine output has fallen. The team want a single blood test to show how severe her tissue hypoperfusion is and to monitor her response to resuscitation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: The test must measure **tissue hypoperfusion** and be repeatable to track resuscitation.

clues: how severe her tissue hypoperfusion is
steps.x: Sepsis with shock and kidney failure: MODS. The question asks for the perfusion marker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lactate**: it rises with anaerobic metabolism and its trend shows response.

elim: Chest X-ray looks for a source; it does not measure perfusion.
CK is for muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis).
D-dimer is non-specific and raised in sepsis anyway.
Troponin assesses myocardial injury, not global perfusion.

steps.x: **A. Lactate.** Rule: in MODS lactate is the critical perfusion marker, repeated to monitor.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man with pneumonia is transferred to intensive care. He has received 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid and IV antibiotics. His pulse rate is 120 bpm, BP 78/44 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 55 mmHg) and urine output is 5 mL per hour. His creatinine is 260 µmol/L and his lactate is 5.0 mmol/L. Bilateral crackles are now heard.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: Next step after fluids and antibiotics in a shocked patient with failing organs.

clues: urine output is 5 mL per hour
steps.x: Persistent shock after adequate fluid, kidneys failing, and crackles mean more fluid will harm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cardiovascular failure despite fluids needs a **vasopressor**: noradrenaline.

elim: Furosemide drops BP further and will not work in shocked kidneys.
Steroids are an add-on only if vasopressors fail, not the next step.
Oral antibiotics are inappropriate in a critically ill patient on IV therapy.
No anaemia or bleeding is described.

steps.x: **C. Noradrenaline.** Rule: circulation failing despite fluids = vasopressors in ICU.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman with severe sepsis from a liver abscess is in intensive care. On a noradrenaline infusion her BP is 118/70 mmHg and pulse rate 96 bpm. Despite this her lactate remains 4.2 mmol/L, she is oliguric and her bilirubin is rising.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her ongoing organ failure?
o: Obstruction of large arteries by emboli

steps.x: A mechanism question: why do organs fail when the BP is normal?
Normal macrocirculation, but tissue is still hypoxic and organs worsen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The cytokine storm damages endothelium, so **microcirculatory flow** fails independent of BP.

elim: Anaphylaxis is an IgE allergic reaction; there is no trigger here.
Antibody deposition causes vasculitis or glomerulonephritis, not sepsis-driven MODS.
Pump failure would give a low BP and pulmonary oedema; her BP is normal.
Large-vessel emboli cause focal ischaemia, not global multi-organ failure.

steps.x: **C. Endothelial damage.** Rule: in MODS the microcirculation fails even when the BP looks fine.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. On day 2 he becomes confused and his urine output falls to 10 mL per hour. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing 6 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pneumonia-driven sepsis with failure of the circulation, kidneys, lungs, liver and brain is MODS. AKI is only one part of the picture.

steps.x: One diagnosis that explains everything.

clues: urine output falls to 10 mL per hour
steps.x: Septic source, then shock, renal, respiratory, liver and neurological failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Two or more organs failing from sepsis: **MODS**.

elim: Retention gives a palpable bladder, not hypoxia and jaundice.
No alcohol history; DTs do not cause renal and liver failure like this.
AKI alone ignores the shock, hypoxia and jaundice.
PE does not explain fever, a pneumonia and rising bilirubin.

steps.x: **C. MODS.** Several organs failing on top of sepsis.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman has a 3 day history of dysuria and loin pain, then rigors. She is now drowsy, hypotensive and oliguric, with a rising creatinine and an oxygen requirement. She has no history of trauma, allergy or recent surgery.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her organ failure?
practice.e: Urinary infection leading to rigors and then multiple organ failure is MODS triggered by sepsis, the commonest cause.

steps.x: The cause of her multi-organ failure, not the name of it.

clues: no history of trauma, allergy or recent surgery
steps.x: A clear infection source followed by failure of several systems.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pyelonephritis caused **sepsis**, the commonest trigger of MODS.

elim: No allergen exposure; anaphylaxis gives wheeze and urticaria.
Hypothyroidism does not cause acute multi-organ failure with rigors.
There is no trauma.
Dehydration alone does not explain rigors and hypoxia.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis.** Sepsis plus organ failure equals MODS.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has MODS secondary to faecal peritonitis. He is confused and breathless and his urine output is falling. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. An arterial blood gas is taken breathing 15 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on arterial blood gas?
practice.e: Hypoperfusion drives anaerobic metabolism, giving a lactic metabolic acidosis, usually with hypoxaemia when the lungs are involved.

steps.x: Predict the gas in a shocked patient with failing organs.
Shock means poor tissue perfusion; fast breathing is compensation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anaerobic metabolism makes lactate: **lactic metabolic acidosis**.

elim: Metabolic alkalosis follows vomiting or diuretics, not shock.
A shocked patient will not have a normal lactate.
He is tachypnoeic, blowing off CO2; acidosis is metabolic.
High bicarbonate is the opposite of a lactic acidosis.

steps.x: **A. Lactic metabolic acidosis.** Raised lactate = poor perfusion.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man is in intensive care 2 days after a motorcycle collision with pelvic and femoral fractures. His haemoglobin is stable. His oxygen requirement is rising, his creatinine has doubled and he is newly jaundiced. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse shadowing.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral diffuse shadowing, normal heart size.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Major trauma can trigger a systemic inflammatory response; lung, kidney, liver and circulatory failure together is MODS. Stable haemoglobin argues against bleeding.

steps.x: One diagnosis for failing lungs, kidneys, liver and circulation.
Trauma is a trigger; several organs now fail together.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Trauma-driven systemic inflammation with multiple organ failure: **MODS**.

elim: Haemoglobin is stable, so bleeding is unlikely.
Contrast nephropathy affects the kidney only.
Pneumonia gives focal consolidation, not liver and kidney failure.
Tension pneumothorax is one-sided with tracheal deviation.

steps.x: **D. MODS.** Trauma, like sepsis, can cause it.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with biliary sepsis is reviewed in intensive care. She has needed noradrenaline for 24 hours, is now on dialysis for acute kidney injury and has just been intubated for respiratory failure. Her daughter asks what most affects her chance of survival.
practice.q: Which feature is most strongly associated with mortality?
practice.e: Mortality in MODS rises sharply with each extra organ system that fails; she has three. Inflammatory markers and fever do not predict death as strongly.

steps.x: A prognosis question about MODS.
Cardiovascular, renal and respiratory failure: three systems.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mortality rises sharply with the **number of organs failed**.

elim: CRP shows inflammation, not prognosis in MODS.
Fever height does not predict death.
Sex is not the key predictor.
White cell count is non-specific.

steps.x: **B. Number of failed organ systems.** Two or more = sharp rise.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has MODS from a perforated duodenal ulcer. A medical student asks which organ systems are most commonly involved. His pulse rate is 120 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on oxygen, and he is oliguric.
practice.q: Which combination of organ systems is most commonly affected in this condition?
practice.e: Respiratory, renal and cardiovascular failure are the commonest in MODS, matching his hypoxia, oliguria and hypotension.

steps.x: Which systems fail most often in MODS?
Circulation, lungs and kidneys are failing in this very stem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiovascular, renal and respiratory**.

elim: Endocrine, skin and bone are not typical MODS systems.
Eye and skin are rarely involved.
Musculoskeletal, eye and ear are not core organ systems in MODS.
Neurological can be involved, but endocrine and skin are not common.

steps.x: **A.** Lungs, kidneys and circulation fail most often.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman with cellulitis becomes hypotensive and confused, with a falling urine output and rising creatinine. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 82/50 mmHg. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to assess the severity of tissue hypoperfusion?
practice.e: Lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion and is repeated to monitor resuscitation; it is the critical test in MODS.

steps.x: The test for severity of hypoperfusion.
Septic shock with organ failure: MODS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lactate**: high lactate = poor perfusion.

elim: A blood film does not assess perfusion.
CT abdomen is not indicated; the source is skin.
Amylase is for pancreatitis.
Dipstick looks for urine infection, not perfusion.

steps.x: **D. Lactate.** The critical blood marker in MODS.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man develops a fever 4 days after a hip replacement, then hypotension, oliguria and a rising bilirubin. The source of infection is not yet clear. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 86/48 mmHg. Antibiotics are about to be started.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: MODS is usually triggered by sepsis; blood cultures before antibiotics (plus imaging) identify the cause and guide treatment.

steps.x: A test to find the cause, before antibiotics.

clues: fever 4 days after a hip replacement
hypotension, oliguria and a rising bilirubin
source of infection is not yet clear
steps.x: Septic MODS with an unknown source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood cultures** before the antibiotics go in.

elim: Marrow biopsy has no role in acute sepsis.
No meningism; LP is not the first test.
Ferritin is non-specific in inflammation.
Thyroid tests do not identify an infection.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Find the cause, then treat it.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with pneumonia is hypotensive, oliguric and hypoxic, with a raised lactate and rising creatinine. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her potassium is 4.9 mmol/L. She has started oxygen and IV fluids.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of the underlying cause?
practice.e: First-line treatment of MODS is treating the cause: IV antibiotics for sepsis. Dialysis is organ support and not needed with a normal potassium.

steps.x: Treat the cause, not an organ.
Septic MODS; supportive steps already begun; no emergency for dialysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV antibiotics** treat the sepsis driving MODS.

elim: Dialysis supports kidneys but does not treat the cause; no urgent indication.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate in a shocked patient.
No low platelets or bleeding described.
Steroids do not treat the infection.

steps.x: **B. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.** Cause first, then organ support.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man in intensive care has MODS from necrotising pancreatitis. He is on noradrenaline and is ventilated. He has passed no urine for 12 hours despite adequate fluids. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg on noradrenaline.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate organ support?
practice.e: Anuric renal failure with hyperkalaemia and acidosis in MODS needs dialysis (renal replacement therapy). Diuretics and resins are too slow or ineffective.

steps.x: Which organ support fits the failing organ?
Anuric kidneys despite fluid; the labs add potassium 6.9 and pH 7.12, so dangerous hyperkalaemia and acidosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Renal failure in MODS = **dialysis** (renal replacement therapy).

elim: Resins act slowly and do not fix acidosis or anuria.
Furosemide will not work in anuric kidneys.
He has had adequate fluid; more risks overload.
Oral bicarbonate is inadequate in a ventilated, anuric patient.

steps.x: **E. Renal replacement therapy.** Kidneys fail = dialysis.

practice.stem: An 84 year old woman with metastatic lung cancer has MODS from pneumonia despite IV antibiotics and fluids. She is now unresponsive and lacks capacity. She has no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 76/42 mmHg. Her son and daughter are at the bedside.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Ask her son to sign a consent form
Discuss escalation versus palliative care with her family
Transfer to ICU for intubation immediately
practice.e: In terminal illness without capacity, discuss escalation versus palliative care with the family to reach an ethical, best-interests decision. Relatives cannot consent without an LPA.

steps.x: A decision about ceiling of care.

clues: no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney
son and daughter are at the bedside
steps.x: Terminal illness, no capacity, family available.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Discuss escalation versus palliative care with the family** and decide in her best interests.

elim: Relatives cannot consent for an adult without an LPA.
Escalation needs a best-interests discussion first.
Courts are for unresolved disputes, not the first step.
Invasive escalation may not be in her best interests; discuss first.

steps.x: **C. Discuss with family.** Capacity first, then a shared best-interests decision.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with MODS from peritonitis is on a noradrenaline infusion. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 120/72 mmHg. Despite this his lactate remains raised and his urine output stays low.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his persistently raised lactate?
practice.e: The cytokine storm damages endothelium, impairing microcirculatory flow independent of BP. Tissues stay hypoxic and switch to anaerobic metabolism, making lactate.

steps.x: Why is lactate high when the BP is normal?
Macrocirculation restored; tissues still under-perfused.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Microcirculatory** failure from endothelial damage.

elim: Diet does not raise lactate like this.
Glucose output does not make lactate rise.
LV failure would cause low BP; his BP is normal.
Noradrenaline is not metabolised to lactate.

steps.x: **A. Endothelial damage.** Normal BP does not mean normal perfusion.

prompts.q: What is MODS and what usually causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: give the number of organs and the trigger.

points.p: Failure of two or more organ systems
points.why: One failed organ is not MODS.

points.p: Usually from a systemic inflammatory response
points.why: SIRS is the phrase exam answers use.

points.p: Sepsis is the commonest trigger (sepsis + organ failure = MODS)
points.why: Trauma and major illness such as pancreatitis also cause it.

prompts.q: Which organ systems are most commonly affected in MODS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the top three.

points.why: Hypoxaemia on ABG; may need ventilation.

prompts.q: How does MODS present at the bedside?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one symptom or sign per organ.

prompts.q: What happens to prognosis as MODS progresses?

points.p: Progression = worsening organ function despite treatment
points.why: This is the sign MODS is advancing.

points.p: Mortality rises sharply once two or more organs fail
points.why: The number of failed organs is the main predictor.

prompts.q: Which processes besides sepsis can trigger MODS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the vignette may start with a non-infectious insult.

points.p: Major illness such as severe pancreatitis
points.why: SIRS and multiorgan dysfunction explain new organ failure after pancreatitis.

prompts.q: How is MODS diagnosed and what is the critical blood test?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: gold standard versus key marker.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis with evidence of organ dysfunction (gold standard)
points.why: There is no single confirmatory test.

prompts.q: Which test shows failure of each organ, and which find the cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match test to organ.

points.p: Arterial blood gas for respiratory failure (hypoxia)
Blood cultures and imaging to find the cause

prompts.q: What is first-line treatment of MODS, and what supportive care is given?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cause first, then support in ICU.

points.p: Treat the cause: antibiotics for sepsis, injury management for trauma
points.why: Antibiotics are the first-line answer for septic MODS.

points.p: ICU supportive care: oxygen or ventilation, IV fluids, vasopressors

prompts.q: Which organ support matches which failing organ?

points.why: Indications include anuria, high potassium, acidosis.
Restore vascular tone when fluids fail.

prompts.q: What do you do about escalation in a patient with MODS and terminal illness?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: capacity, then family discussion.

points.p: If lacking capacity, discuss escalation versus palliative care with the family
points.why: Aim for an ethically and legally appropriate, unanimous decision; relatives cannot consent without an LPA.

prompts.q: Why do organs fail in MODS, even when the BP is normal?

points.p: Systemic inflammation causes microvascular dysfunction and reduced tissue perfusion
Cytokine storm damages endothelium throughout the body
Organs are interconnected: e.g. renal failure causes fluid overload, worsening respiratory failure

prompts.q: Why is lactate raised in MODS and why is it repeated?

points.p: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery causes a shift to anaerobic metabolism
Its trend monitors response to resuscitation
points.why: A falling lactate means perfusion is improving.

glossary.MODS: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome: failure of two or more organ systems, usually from systemic inflammation such as sepsis.
glossary.SIRS: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome: a body-wide inflammatory reaction to infection, trauma or major illness.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
glossary.Septic shock: Sepsis with persistent hypotension despite adequate fluids, needing vasopressors.
glossary.Lactate: Product of anaerobic metabolism; a raised level shows tissue hypoperfusion.
glossary.Hypoperfusion: Not enough blood flow to deliver oxygen to tissues.
glossary.Microcirculation: Blood flow through the smallest vessels (arterioles, capillaries, venules) where oxygen reaches cells.
glossary.Macrocirculation: Flow in the large vessels, reflected by blood pressure and cardiac output.
glossary.Endothelium: The single cell layer lining blood vessels; damaged by cytokines in sepsis.
glossary.Cytokine storm: Excessive release of inflammatory signalling proteins that damages tissues throughout the body.
glossary.Capillary leak: Fluid escaping from damaged small vessels into tissues, causing oedema and low circulating volume.
glossary.Anaerobic metabolism: Energy production without oxygen; makes lactate as a by-product.
glossary.Vasopressor: Drug that constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure, e.g. noradrenaline.
glossary.Noradrenaline: First-line vasopressor in septic shock; given by infusion in ICU.
glossary.Dialysis: Renal replacement therapy that removes waste, potassium, acid and fluid when the kidneys fail.
glossary.Renal replacement therapy: Dialysis or haemofiltration used to take over kidney function.
glossary.Mechanical ventilation: A machine breathes for the patient through an endotracheal tube.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, pH, bicarbonate and lactate.
glossary.ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: inflammatory lung injury with bilateral shadowing and severe hypoxaemia.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid fall in kidney function with rising creatinine or falling urine output.
glossary.Oliguria: Low urine output, under about 0.5 mL/kg per hour.
glossary.Creatinine: Waste product cleared by the kidneys; a rising level means falling kidney function.
glossary.Bilirubin: Breakdown product of haem cleared by the liver; raised in hepatic injury.
glossary.Hypoxaemia: Low oxygen level in arterial blood.
glossary.MAP: Mean arterial pressure; the target in shock is usually 65 mmHg or above.
glossary.ICU: Intensive care unit, where organ support is given.
glossary.Capacity: The ability to understand, retain, weigh up information and communicate a decision.
glossary.LPA: Lasting power of attorney: a legal document letting a named person make decisions if capacity is lost.
glossary.Palliative care: Care focused on comfort and quality of life rather than cure.
glossary.Ceiling of care: The agreed upper limit of treatment escalation for a patient.
glossary.Best interests: The standard for decisions made for an adult who lacks capacity, under the Mental Capacity Act.
glossary.Ascending cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, often from obstruction; classic fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
glossary.Sepsis Six: Bundle completed within 1 hour: oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output.
glossary.Faecal peritonitis: Infection of the peritoneum from bowel contents after a perforation.
